title: Why salt dissolves in water but sand doesn't
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why does salt dissolve in water?
Where does salt go when it dissolves?

explain.say: Stir salt into water and it seems to vanish, but stir in sand and it just sinks. The difference is in how strongly water can pull on their particles.

draw.text: Why salt dissolves in water but sand doesn't

explain.say: Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: a salt crystal lattice. Look at the sodium ion, the chloride ion and the ionic bond. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: Why salt dissolves in water but sand doesn't

explain.say: Salt is made of charged particles called ions, sodium and chloride. Water molecules are slightly charged at each end, so they crowd round the ions and pull them out of the crystal one by one.
Sand is mostly quartz, in which every atom is joined to its neighbours by very strong bonds in one giant network. Water cannot pull those bonds apart, so the sand stays solid.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Water only dissolves what it can pull apart

explain.say: Even salt has a limit: about 36 grams dissolve in 100 millilitres of water at room temperature, while sugar dissolves far more. Then the solution is saturated.

draw.name: x-sizes
draw.unit: grams in 100 ml of water at 20 °C

faq.q: What happens to salt when it dissolves?
faq.a: Water molecules surround the sodium and chloride ions and pull them away from the crystal, spreading them evenly through the water. They are too small to see.
Sand is mostly quartz, silicon dioxide, held together by very strong bonds in a giant network. Water molecules cannot pull it apart.
No. The salt is still there, spread out as ions. You can taste it, and if you let the water evaporate, the salt crystals come back.

faq.q: Does hot water dissolve more salt?
faq.a: A little more. Hot water dissolves only slightly more salt than cold water, but it dissolves much more sugar.

faq.q: Is there a limit to how much salt dissolves?
faq.a: Yes. About 36 grams of salt dissolve in 100 millilitres of water at room temperature. After that the solution is saturated and extra salt sits at the bottom.

facts: About 36 grams of table salt dissolve in 100 millilitres of water at 20 degrees Celsius.
About 200 grams of sugar dissolve in 100 millilitres of water at 20 degrees Celsius.
